entries.proposition: Design: 15 male Wistar rats, 8 on standard chow and 7 on a ketogenic diet for 60 days, caged singly, food ad libitum.
entries.snippet: Rats were divided into two groups. The first group (n = 8) received a standard diet, while the second group received the ketogenic diet for 60 days.

experimental_context.system: healthy adult male Wistar rats, 60 days of home-made high-fat diet versus standard chow (n = 7 versus 8), single terminal blood sample
experimental_context.endpoint: blood gas, haematology, liver and kidney markers, MDA, SOD

entries.proposition: Table 1 note: the in-house diet is built on a fat to (carbohydrate plus protein) ratio of 8.6 to 1, from goat fat, egg yolk, avocado and peanuts.
entries.snippet: Formula is prepared based on ketogenic diet for rats, with the ratio of 8.6 : 1 portion of fat:(carbohydrate + protein) [16].

entries.snippet: It was found there was a very significant decrease in blood pH of rats following 2 months of having a ketogenic diet compared to those fed with a standard diet (p < 0.01).

entries.snippet: However, this complication of the ketogenic diet can be managed with copper supplementation.

entries.proposition: Liver and kidney function markers did not differ significantly; creatinine and urea were somewhat higher in ketogenic rats.
entries.snippet: However, when comparing the renal function test, a slight increase in plasma creatinine and urea levels was found in the ketogenic group compared to standard, although the difference was not statistically significant.

entries.proposition: Oxidative stress: tissue malondialdehyde rose (very significant) and plasma SOD fell about 80 percent in ketogenic rats; MDA and SOD measured once at end point.
entries.snippet: The increase of MDA level in the ketogenic group was accompanied by a reduced level of antioxidant superoxide dismutase (SOD), which was ∼80% lower compared to that of standard (p < 0.01).
